source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part III: The First Hour (The Opening Range) (introduction)

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same. Helpers: isFirstBarOfSession(n) as in V17-01; isNthBarOfSession(n, k) = bar[n] is the (k+1)-th bar of its session (session-start offset == k); ema/emaSlope(n, lookback) = ema[n]-ema[n+lookback]; overlapFraction(n) = overlap between bar[n] and bar[n+1] as a fraction of bar[n]'s range; doji(n) = body(n) fraction of range below dojiBodyFraction; tailFraction(n) = larger of the two wick fractions of bar[n]'s range; bullTrendBar(n)/bearTrendBar(n) = body-fraction test; averageDailyRange(N) = average of (high-low) over the N prior sessions; consecutiveTrendBarSpike(startOffset, n, dir) as in V19-02.

candidates.name: FadeNonDojiBarAfterMove
candidates.quote: they avoid doji signal bars, but will often short below either a bull or a bear trend bar after a move up, or buy above a bull or a bear trend bar after a move down.
candidates.description: In the opening range, after a move up over the last few bars, fade the next non-doji bar (bull or bear body) by shorting one tick below its low; mirrored for a move down.
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick below the signal bar's low (short) / above its high (long)

complexity.reason: needs a 'move up/down over the last few bars' measure plus a non-doji test; no pivot detection

notes: 'a move up' has no precise Brooks definition here; moveBars/moveTicks are readings.

candidates.name: VolatilityScaledStopDistance
candidates.quote: When the bars are big, traders should use wider stops and trade smaller size.
candidates.description: Scale the protective stop distance beyond the signal bar to a multiple of the signal bar's own range (or a short-lookback ATR), rather than a fixed tick amount, when opening-range bars are unusually large.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop beyond the signal bar, sized to the bar's own range

complexity.reason: a per-trade stop distance derived from a single bar's range rather than a fixed constant; position-sizing half of the guideline (trade smaller size) is not representable as an Entry/Exit/Switch condition and is omitted

notes: Only the stop-distance half of 'wider stops and smaller size' is mechanizable in this rule-role system; position sizing is not.

candidates.name: YesterdayCloseAlwaysInCarriesOverBias
candidates.quote: Yesterday's always-in direction going into the close often carries over into the open of today.
candidates.description: Context filter: if yesterday's session closed in a clear always-in direction, bias today's opening entries toward that same direction until price action contradicts it.

complexity.reason: 'always-in direction' is the trilogy's own example of a concept needing a design decision before it can be coded; this is that same primitive read at yesterday's close and carried forward

notes: Mirrors the AlwaysInDirection primitive pattern used elsewhere in the trilogy (e.g. the trends volume's front matter).

candidates.name: FirstBarDojiImpliesTwoSidedDay
candidates.quote: If the first bar is a doji or the first several bars overlap and have prominent tails, the day is more likely to have lots of two-sided trading.
candidates.description: Context filter: the first bar of the session is a doji -- raises the odds of a two-sided/trading-range day, favoring fade setups over breakout continuation.

complexity.reason: session-boundary primitive plus a single-bar doji test

notes: A simpler, standalone version of chapter 19's V19-07, which additionally required the bar to sit inside yesterday's closing range.

candidates.name: EmaFlatFilter
candidates.quote: If it is a doji in the middle of a tight trading range from the final hour of yesterday and the moving average is flat, the odds favor a trading range day.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the EMA has moved less than a small tick threshold over the last N bars -- 'the moving average is flat', used to reinforce a trading-range-day read.

complexity.reason: a difference of two EMA readings compared to a tick threshold

notes: Composes with FirstBarDojiImpliesTwoSidedDay (VP3-04) and yesterday's-closing-range tests to reproduce the book's full first-bar read.

candidates.name: SecondBarBreakoutOfFirstBar
candidates.quote: Traders often enter on the second bar of the day as it breaks beyond the high or low of the first bar.
candidates.description: The second bar of the session closes beyond the high (long) / low (short) of the first bar of the session: enter in that direction.
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick above the first bar's high (long) / below its low (short)

complexity.reason: session-boundary primitive plus a single fixed-offset comparison

notes: Brooks explicitly flags this as usually a losing trader's equation for a scalp but a reasonable swing setup on the rare high-probability day (e.g. large gap plus a strong first bar); recorded as the bare entry condition, sizing/management left to the authoring pass.

candidates.name: DoubleBottomFlagAfterOpenSpike
candidates.quote: if there is a series of strong bull trend bars off the open and then a partial pullback that gets tested five to 10 bars later, this forms a double bottom flag entry and has a good chance of leading to a new high of the day.
candidates.description: After a series of strong bull trend bars off the open, a partial pullback whose low is tested again 5-10 bars later forms a double-bottom-flag long entry.
candidates.pseudocode: consecutiveTrendBarSpike(pullbackAge, spikeBars, up) && isDoubleBottom(0, testWindowMin, testWindowMax)
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick above the second-bottom bar's high (long) / below the second-top bar's low (short)

complexity.reason: depends on a double-bottom detection primitive (swing-pivot based) on top of the multi-bar spike primitive

notes: isDoubleBottom is a placeholder for the primitive defined in this book's earlier double top/bottom chapter (chapter 8, not in this mining batch).

candidates.name: WaitAfterReportTimeFilter
candidates.quote: Most traders should not trade in the seconds after a report but should wait for the price action to return to normal, which often takes one to about 10 minutes.
candidates.description: Context filter: block new entries within a short window after a known scheduled-report time (e.g. 7:00 a.m. PST), when algorithmic/HFT activity dominates price action.

complexity.reason: a plain bar-close-time comparison against a fixed scheduled time, though the exact report time is market/session dependent

notes: Reasoning (algorithmic order-flow speed advantage) is not observable data, but the clock-time suppression window itself is directly decidable, similar in shape to the existing TimeWindow rule.

candidates.name: FadeFirstBarWithProminentTailsBreakout
candidates.quote: If the bar is a trend bar but has prominent tails, it is a one-bar trading range... many traders will short above the bar and buy below the bar for a scalp, since they know that reversals usually dominate the first hour and that the breakout of a trading range, even if the trading range is a single bar, is likely to fail.
candidates.description: The first bar of the session has prominent tails (a body that does not dominate its range): treat it as a one-bar trading range and fade breakouts of it -- short one tick above its high, buy one tick below its low.
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick above the first bar's high (short) / below its low (long) -- a fade, opposite direction to the breakout

complexity.reason: session-boundary primitive plus a tail-fraction test and a fixed-offset breakout comparison

notes: This is a fade (opposite direction to the breakout of the level), distinct from VP3-06 which trades WITH the breakout of the first bar.

candidates.name: ScalpLimitAtSpikeLowAfterConsecutiveTrendBars
candidates.quote: if there are two consecutive strong bull trend bars and then a doji bar, they might place limit orders to buy at or below the low of the doji bar. Since they see it as a weak reversal signal, especially after such a strong bull spike, they expect it to fail.
candidates.description: After N consecutive strong bull trend bars, place a resting limit order to buy at or below the low of the first weak pullback bar that follows (a doji or an opposite-colored bar), betting that the pullback fails and the bull spike resumes.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at or below the pullback bar's low (long) / at or above its high (short) -- not a stop entry

complexity.reason: the multi-bar spike primitive plus a touch-level limit-order test; the limit fill is approximated by the bar's low/high trading through the level

notes: Explicitly a limit entry, not the book's usual stop-beyond-signal-bar convention; kept as a touch-of-level test since the engine cannot see intrabar order priority.

candidates.name: ThirdBarBreakoutSignificance
candidates.quote: The first 15 minute bar closes at the close of the third 5 minute bar... trading the breakout of the third bar of the day often leads to a big move.
candidates.description: Context filter: on a 5-minute chart, a breakout of the third bar of the session carries extra weight because it coincides with the close of the first 15-minute bar; treat a breakout of that bar's high/low as higher-confidence than an ordinary bar breakout.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (confidence-weighting filter on an otherwise ordinary breakout entry)

complexity.reason: requires a 'third bar of session' offset test on top of a fixed-offset breakout comparison; specific to charts built from 5-minute bars

notes: Only meaningful when the strategy's own bar interval is 5 minutes (so that 3 bars align with a 15-minute close); on other intervals this candidate does not apply as stated.

candidates.name: HolidayWeekRangeDayBias
candidates.quote: When trading around holidays like Christmas week and the week of the Fourth of July, the first hour is often very important because often that is the only time when the market behaves like a normal day. It then frequently enters a tight trading range for the rest of the day.
candidates.description: Context filter: during specific holiday weeks (Christmas week, the week of July 4th), expect normal price action only in the first hour and a tight trading range for the rest of the session.

complexity.reason: a calendar-date test, computable on any bar interval including daily, though the described behavior (quiet after the first hour) is an intraday effect

notes: Date ranges are a reading of 'Christmas week' and 'the week of the Fourth of July'; not given precisely by Brooks.

candidates.name: BarOverlapMidCloseBarbwireSignal
candidates.quote: By the third bar of the day, barbwire was likely because about half of its range was overlapped by the prior bar and it closed in its middle, meaning that the following bar would also likely overlap about half of its range.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a bar overlaps at least half of its range with the prior bar and closes near the middle of its own range -- an onset signal for barbwire (tight, two-sided trading), predicting the next bar is also likely to overlap heavily.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification feeding a two-sided-trading context filter)

complexity.reason: a windowless overlap-fraction comparison between two adjacent bars plus a close-position-in-range test

notes: This is a candidate definition for the 'barbwire' primitive referenced throughout the chapter but not itself defined here in numeric terms until this passage.

candidates.name: LowRangeStockScalpAvoidance
candidates.quote: Traders should not often scalp stocks with average daily ranges under a dollar, but price action entries still work.
candidates.description: Context filter: when the instrument's recent average daily range is below a small dollar (or tick) threshold, avoid scalp-sized targets; price-action entries can still be taken but should be managed for a swing instead.

complexity.reason: a rolling average-range comparison against a fixed dollar threshold

notes: 'A dollar' is instrument-price-scale specific (this is written for stocks); on futures/forex the threshold would need to be in the instrument's own units.

candidates.name: SteepEmaSlopeSellOffReversal
candidates.quote: Whenever the moving average is as steeply up as it was yesterday, any strong sell-off below it will almost always be followed by a tradable rally back up.
candidates.description: If the EMA had a steep up-slope in a recent session and price makes a strong sell-off below the current EMA, expect (and enter on) a reversal rally back up.
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick above the reversal bar's high (long) / below its low (short)

complexity.reason: combines an EMA-slope measurement from a prior session with a same-day distance-below-EMA test and a reversal-bar test; the specific thresholds are not given by Brooks

notes: Composes with EmaFlatFilter (VP3-05) as the opposite-slope case (steep vs. flat).

candidates.name: CountOfReversalsInFirstHourImpliesRangeDay
candidates.quote: If dojis continue and there are five reversals in the first hour, the odds of a trading range day go up.
candidates.description: Context filter: counting five or more reversal bars within the first hour of the session raises the odds of a trading-range day, favoring fade setups over breakout continuation for the rest of the session.

complexity.reason: 'reversal' is not defined numerically in this passage; a design decision is needed for what counts as one before this can be coded

notes: countReversalBars is a placeholder for whichever reversal-bar primitive the authoring pass settles on (likely defined in this book's signal-bar chapters, not in this mining batch).

rejected.quote: The location of the open of the day is not set by any firm or group of firms; instead, it represents a brief equilibrium between buyers and sellers... If the institutions have a large amount of buying planned for the day, why would the market ever open a stock above yesterday's close and then sell off before rallying to a new high?
rejected.reason: extended narrative about unobservable institutional order-flow motives and intentions; not decidable from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: About 70 percent of all trading is automated... Dow Jones & Company now has a news service called Lexicon that transmits machine-readable financial news to its subscribers... Some programs use differential evolution optimizing software to generate data that is used to generate other data.
rejected.reason: requires knowledge of other market participants' algorithms, news feeds, and computing infrastructure -- data the engine does not have and cannot infer from its own OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: scalpers generally have to win on 60 percent or more of their trades, since the risk usually has to be about the size of the reward... For example, if they average two profitable scalps a day of two points each and trade 25 Emini contracts, they could make a million dollars a year.
rejected.reason: illustrative trader's-equation arithmetic (probability/risk/reward worked examples) for a specific hypothetical trader, not a generalizable bar-level test

rejected.quote: Bar 1 was the third bar of the day and it was a small bull reversal bar. It reversed up from the moving average and a swing low from yesterday... Bar 9 was the first of a two-bar bull spike after the higher low.
rejected.reason: extended bar-by-bar figure narration (Figures PIII.1-PIII.4) is discretionary chart commentary on specific historical charts; the recurring named patterns it applies (two-bar reversal, low 2/high 2, double top/bottom, wedge, micro channel, spike and climax, trend line breaks) are primitives expected from other chapters of this book, not redefined here

chapter_summary: Part III's introduction is largely a discursive essay on why the opening range is both the easiest time to make and lose money, on distinguishing scalp from swing trader's-equation math, and on unobservable institutional order-flow and algorithmic-trading narratives (all rejected). Underneath that, it yields a useful set of concrete opening-bar and first-hour primitives and filters: fading non-doji bars after a move, a volatility-scaled stop, an always-in carryover bias from yesterday's close, first-bar doji/flat-EMA range-day classifiers, a second-bar and a third-bar breakout entry, a double-bottom-flag-after-open-spike pattern, a report-time entry-suppression window, a fade-the-first-bar-with-tails pattern, a limit-order scalp after consecutive trend bars, a holiday-week calendar filter, a numeric barbwire-onset definition (bar overlap plus mid-range close), a low-range-stock scalp-avoidance filter, a steep-EMA-slope reversal setup, and a reversal-count range-day filter. Several candidates (VP3-03, VP3-07, VP3-15, VP3-16) are intentionally soft/research- or hard-grade because the underlying concepts (always-in, double bottom, reversal bar counting) are primitives this book defines more precisely elsewhere; the four bar-by-bar figures at the end reuse those same named patterns and were not mined individually.
